en.marketHeading: What is actually different about marketing in {city}
market: Most bilingual marketing advice in Canada is really advice about Montreal, where the answer is to lead in French. Greater {city} is a different situation, because the population here is genuinely mixed rather than tilted decisively one way. An English-only campaign is invisible to a large part of the market, and a French-only one is invisible to another large part. Running both is not a nicety in this city, it is the difference between addressing your market and addressing some of it.

That has a practical cost most people underestimate. Two languages means two sets of keywords, two sets of ads, two landing pages and two conversations with whoever answers your phone. Half-doing it, which usually means machine-translating the English and hoping, reads badly to francophone customers and tends to convert worse than not bothering. I would rather scope it properly or leave it English-only on purpose than ship something that quietly insults a third of your prospects.

The second thing about {city} is that it is where Atlantic Canada's freight and distribution converge, and where a lot of national contact-centre and back-office work landed. Businesses here routinely serve New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and beyond from one address. Targeting only {city} is often far too narrow, and the region grew 8.9% between the last two censuses against 5.2% nationally, so the local base is expanding underneath that too.

faq.q: Do you have an office in {city}?
faq.a: No. I am based in Toronto and work from home, so there is no {city} office and I am not going to imply there is. Everything is run remotely over video and email, which is how I run every account. If you want someone who will walk into your shop, I am the wrong hire and I will say so on the call rather than after you have paid.

I can build and run the French side of a campaign, and I will be straight with you about the limit: I am not a native French speaker, so any French copy I produce should be reviewed by someone who is before it goes live. For a market like {city} I would rather budget for that review than pretend it is unnecessary. If you already have a francophone on staff, that is usually the cheapest and best answer.

faq.q: Can we just translate our English ads?
faq.a: You can, and it usually underperforms. People do not search for translations of English phrases, they search for how the thing is actually said, and the wording that converts in one language is rarely a direct rendering of the other. Separate keyword research per language is the part that actually pays for itself.

faq.q: Should we target all of Atlantic Canada?
faq.a: If you genuinely serve it, yes, and many {city} businesses do because of where the distribution networks run. If you are a local trade or a restaurant, no. The test is simple: can you actually deliver to a customer in Halifax or Charlottetown at a price that works.

Google Ads management is $1,500 a month plus your ad spend. SEO consulting is $1,200 a month. AIO consulting is $1,800 one time. No setup fees and no long contract. Running two languages properly takes more work than one, and I will tell you what that means for scope before you commit to anything.
